extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, Patent Office examiners, and courts (U.S. patent practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards for when and how a U.S. patent (letters-patent) may be amended by surrender and re-issue: what defects may be corrected, limits on enlarging claims, required state of mind (inadvertence/mistake), timeliness, and interaction with the original specification/drawings/models and third-party rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same invention requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issued patent must be for the same invention as the original patent; if the re-issued patent is for a different invention the re-issue is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts repeatedly hold the re-issued patent must cover the same invention as originally patented. The patentee may 'redescribe his invention, and include in the Description and Claims ... whatever else was suggested or substantially indicated in the old specification, drawings, or Patent-Office model which properly belonged to the invention.' The jury may look to the original drawings to determine whether the inventions are the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: No enlargement of the invention (general prohibition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue cannot enlarge or expand the Claims of the original patent; re-issue is not permitted to enlarge the original right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous cases (e.g., Dunbar v. White and others cited) assert that enlargement of the original claims by re-issue makes the re-issue void. However, courts differ in borderline situations; enlargement may be permitted only in narrow circumstances (see other metrics about inadvertence, promptness, and lack of intervening rights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction for inadvertence, accident, or mistake
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-issue is available when the Description or the Claim is inexact or incomplete, or when the Claim is broader than the actual invention, provided the error arose from 'inadvertence, accident, or mistake' and without fraudulent or deceptive intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central statutory/ equitable ground for reissues: the error must be bona fide and inadvertent. The treatise summarizes: the act confers the privilege of a re-issue whenever the Description or the Claim is inexact or incomplete, or when the Claim is broader than the actual invention, provided the error stems from inadvertence/accident/mistake and not from fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual bona fide mistake required (not mere error of judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'actual mistake' (a bona fide inadvertent error) is required for an enlarging re-issue; mere error of judgment (which can be corrected on appeal) does not qualify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts distinguish between mistakes of judgment (not grounds for re-issue) and inadvertent mistakes of fact in the specification/claim. The remedy is available where a court of chancery would have corrected the mistake — an actual inadvertence, not an after-the-fact change of mind or litigation strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promptness / no unreasonable delay / laches / intervening rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee must apply for re-issue promptly; unreasonable delay, laches, or intervening rights (including public appropriation of unclaimed matter or third-party investments) may defeat a re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many decisions refuse re-issues where the patentee 'slept upon his rights' or delayed until others had invested in the art. Unreasonable delay suggests the claim of original inadvertence is a pretence. Courts balance equities; even when statutory conditions are present, a re-issue may be denied if it prejudices others or the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: No new matter / no material addition of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue cannot add material subject matter that constitutes a new invention that was not described, suggested, or substantially indicated in the original specification, drawings, or Patent-Office model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patentee may not 'make material additions to the invention which were not described, suggested, nor substantially indicated in the original specifications, drawings, or Patent-Office model.' Re-issue may correct or clarify, but cannot introduce 'new matter' that enlarges the invention beyond what was originally disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim as part of the specification — amendability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Claim is an essential part of the specification and is amendable by re-issue to correct defects of undue restriction, excess, inexactness, or insufficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically the claim (whether in grant language or petition language) has always been part of the specification and subject to the same kinds of defects as the descriptive part; therefore claims may be limited, clarified, or otherwise amended by re-issue to correct inadvertent defects. Courts recognize both undue restriction (claim too narrow) and undue excess (claim too broad) as correctable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue is the appropriate mode to secure accidentally omitted subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Where matter that belonged to the invention was accidentally omitted from the original patent, re-issue is the proper (and sometimes the only) mode to secure that subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions (e.g., Keystone Bridge v. Phoenix Iron Co. and others cited) hold that re-issue is the appropriate (and in some formulations the only) remedy for inadvertently omitted features that were part of the original invention as shown in the specification/drawings/models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings/models/drawings evidence may justify claim changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements shown in original drawings or models, even if not expressly claimed, can support inclusion in a re-issue if they were part of the original invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will look to drawings and models to determine if an element was part of the original invention; if so, the patentee (or assignee) may incorporate that element into the re-issued patent. The jury may examine drawings to determine identity of inventions covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable/public-interest balancing — re-issue may be denied
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when statutory requirements are met, courts may deny re-issue based on equitable considerations where the public or intervening patentees would be unjustly prejudiced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise emphasizes that re-issue powers are granted for inventor protection but are not absolute: courts may refuse re-issue when it would unfairly appropriate the discovery without consideration, unduly prejudice others, or work a forfeiture of intervening rights. Laches and public appropriation are key equitable bars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner/Patent Office discretion to insert new claims founded on original invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute authorizes the Patent Office (Commissioner) to allow insertion of new claims founded on the original invention when omission results from inadvertence, accident, or mistake, and when the claimant has not estopped himself from exercising the right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (e.g., Seymour v. Osborne) recognize express authority for the Commissioner to entertain applications to insert new claims based on original disclosure when omission was inadvertent and the patentee is not estopped. The power has been construed liberally in favor of inventors, subject to intervening rights and estoppel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicting authorities on claiming described-but-unclaimed matter
rubrics_metrics.description: There is tension in authority: some decisions assert a re-issue cannot claim what was described but not claimed in the original (e.g., Reed v. Chase), while many other courts have held re-issue is the proper mode to secure what was described but not claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise records this split in authority and indicates that later and numerous cases permit securing described-but-unclaimed elements by re-issue when they clearly belonged to the original invention, especially if the applicant acts promptly and no intervening rights exist. Practitioners must consider jurisdiction and precedent.
